To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
aluminium is present within human breast tissue and fluids and that there is a correlation between aluminium levels and the presence of human breast cancer.

aluminium is present at higher levels in the breast tissue and microenvironment of women diagnosed with breast cancer, compared with healthy subjects, and is associated with raised levels of proteins and mRNA that modulate intracellular calcium levels and iron homeostasis.

aluminium is present at higher levels in the breast of breast cancer patients and in type I cyst fluid, and is associated with overexpression of proteins that modulates iron homeostasis and S100 calcium binding protein in breast cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the biological significance of the presence of aluminium in the breast and the possible role of aluminium as an etiological factor in the development of breast cancer.
the role of aluminium in the development of breast cancer.
understanding the biological significance of aluminium in human breast tissues and fluids, with a particular interest in the possible relationship between aluminium and breast cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the presence of aluminium in breast tissue and fluids is a fact.
aluminium is present within the breast, but its role in breast diseases is unclear and requires further investigation.
aluminium is present at higher levels in the human breast in vivo when cancer is present, and in human breast cysts in vitro.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

aluminium is present within breast tissue and breast fluids at raised levels in the presence of breast disease, and that aluminium exposure in vitro alters expression of proteins that may modulate calcium homeostasis and/or iron homeostasis.
aluminium is present at increased levels in breast tissues of breast cancer patients and that it is possible that aluminium is involved in the pathogenesis of breast cancer.
there are increased levels of aluminium present in breast tissue, nipple aspirate fluids, and breast cyst fluids.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the human breast is exposed and responds to the presence of aluminium.
aluminium may play a role in the development and/or maintenance of breast disease and that further investigation is required to determine the biological impact of aluminium in the breast.
aluminium is a potential risk factor for development of human breast diseases, and further studies are required to establish whether aluminium is a causative agent.
